question: Can one simulator-trained deep reinforcement-learning policy replace the nested magnetic-control stack of a tokamak, directly command all 19 TCV coils at 10 kHz, and transfer without weight tuning across substantially different plasma-current, position, boundary-shape, X-point, and multi-plasma objectives?

key_findings.claim: The work demonstrates an unusually broad integrated magnetic-control interface: one learned policy consumes raw magnetic and coil-current measurements plus time-varying targets and commands every active TCV coil.
key_findings.evidence: The deployed policy receives 34 flux-loop readings, 38 magnetic-probe readings, 19 active-coil currents, and the difference between the two ohmic-coil currents, for 92 measurements, together with as many as 132 target values. It directly outputs commands for 19 coils. This is substantially broader than the cited earlier RL applications to one profile or a feedforward beta signal.

key_findings.claim: The central empirical result is zero-shot simulator-to-TCV transfer after conventional plasma formation, not online reinforcement learning on the tokamak.
key_findings.evidence: MPO learns entirely from interaction with FGE simulations. Each plant experiment begins under conventional formation and ramp-up control, switches to a compiled deterministic neural policy at a prespecified handover, and uses no plant-side network-weight tuning. The tokamak supplies neither reward nor policy updates during deployment.

key_findings.claim: The fundamental-capability shot tracks a demanding sequence of current, elongation, vertical displacement, triangularity, and diverted-shape targets with sub-kiloampere and roughly centimetre-scale aggregate errors.
key_findings.evidence: For TCV shot 70915 over the 0.1-1.0 s control interval, Extended Data Table 1 gives plasma-current RMSE 0.62 kA and LCFS-shape RMSE 0.75 cm. The initial limited phase gives 0.71 kA and 0.78 cm, and the diverted phase gives 0.28 kA and 0.53 cm. Figure 2 shows the corresponding reference and post-shot reconstruction traces.

key_findings.claim: Separate learned controllers produce four advanced single-plasma configurations on hardware, including a highly elongated plasma, an ITER-like H-mode shape, strong negative triangularity, and a controllably merging snowflake.
key_findings.evidence: TCV 70920 reaches elongation 1.9 despite an instability growth rate above 1.4 kHz; TCV 70600 operates with neutral-beam heating and beta_p up to 1.12; TCV 70457 targets triangularity -0.8; and TCV 70755 moves the X-point separation from 34 cm to 6.6 cm. Reported aggregate errors include 1.2 kA/1.6 cm for the elongated case, 2.6 kA/1.4 cm for the ITER-like case, 3.5 kA/1.3 cm for negative triangularity, and 0.50 kA/0.65 cm with 3.7 cm combined X-point error for the snowflake.

key_findings.claim: The two-droplet experiment is a striking qualitative extension, but it is not supported by the same quantitative tracking table as the single-plasma shots.
key_findings.evidence: TCV 69545 maintains two visually distinct, independently current-targeted plasma lobes for the full 200 ms control window. Figure 4 supplies current traces and a vessel photograph, but Extended Data Table 1 contains no droplet row and the text reports no per-lobe shape, position, or current RMSE.

key_findings.claim: The architecture deliberately spends capacity during training while keeping the deployed actor small enough for a 50-microsecond real-time budget.
key_findings.evidence: The 718,337-parameter critic uses a 256-wide LSTM and two 256-wide MLP layers, whereas the 266,280-parameter policy is feedforward with LayerNorm, tanh, and three 256-wide ELU layers. Extended Data Figure 5 shows that merely widening a feedforward critic to 512 or 1,024 units does not match the recurrent critic. Only the deterministic action mean is compiled and deployed at 10 kHz.

anchors.section: Methods / Asymmetric critic and learning loop

key_findings.claim: Training is computationally substantial despite the small deployed controller, and the paper does not report a normalized compute or energy comparison with conventional controller design.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments use 5,000 parallel simulator actors and one TPU learner, typically for 1-3 days and sometimes longer. The actor-count ablation shows that 100 actors can learn basic stabilization nearly as fast and 20 actors can reach similar reward in roughly two days, but all reported experiment policies use 5,000 actors. No total simulator steps, TPU-hours, energy, engineering-hours, or conventional-design cost is tabulated.

key_findings.claim: The paper establishes feasibility on real hardware, but not a statistically characterized advantage over conventional, model-predictive, or expert-designed control.
key_findings.evidence: Each headline configuration is represented by one named shot. Extended Data Figure 3 shows two repeated ITER-like shots before their heating conditions diverge, but there are no repeated-shot means, confidence intervals, failure rates, matched conventional-controller runs, or randomized comparisons. The conventional design appears conceptually in Figure 1 rather than as an experimental performance baseline.

key_findings.claim: Several reported boundary-shape errors are close to the scale of the post-shot reconstruction used to score them.
key_findings.evidence: The learned controller does not run LIUQE in its real-time loop, but LIUQE reconstructs the LCFS and X-points after each shot and supplies initial equilibria for training. The Methods state typical boundary accuracy is about 1 cm, while reported shape RMSE values span 0.53-1.6 cm. Thus small differences among the best shape results should not be read as substantially finer than the evaluation instrument without uncertainty propagation.

key_findings.claim: The design remains heavily model- and reward-engineered, so descriptions of it as simply model-free or requiring minimal design effort need qualification.
key_findings.evidence: Policy optimization is model-free at the MPO interface, but the engineering pipeline depends on a device-specific free-boundary physics simulator, identified sensor and actuator models, parameter-domain randomization, hand-specified targets, per-experiment reward terms and weights, and explicit rewards for learned-region avoidance and invalid external X-points. Extended Data Tables 2-5 document substantial device and task specification rather than a single reward reused unchanged.

anchors.section: Methods / Simulator, parameter variation, sensing and actuation

key_findings.claim: The simulator deliberately omits transport physics that become important for heated, high-performance, or long-horizon operation.
key_findings.evidence: FGE assumes axisymmetric Grad-Shafranov equilibrium and circuit dynamics. It does not model radial pressure and current-density transport from heating or current drive, instead using polynomial profiles parameterized by beta_p and q_A plus a lumped current-evolution equation. Droplets are treated as pressureless, disable the G coil, and use an earlier plasma-current model. Successful transfer on the demonstrated shots does not validate omitted transport dynamics or a universal simulator fidelity claim.

anchors.section: Methods / Tokamak simulator and specific settings for droplets

key_findings.claim: Deployment still needs conventional startup control and an independent safety layer; the learned controller is not claimed to guarantee disruption avoidance.
key_findings.evidence: The authors require an existing controller for breakdown and early current ramp-up. They explicitly state that simulation termination penalties do not guarantee disruption avoidance and recommend a fallback controller or interlock when a device cannot tolerate particular disruptions. The termination conditions themselves are heuristic operational bounds, including q95 below 2.2, coil limits, an ohmic-coil difference limit, and low plasma current.

key_findings.claim: The accompanying artifact is a tested, informative partial release but cannot reproduce training or the plant experiments end to end.
key_findings.evidence: The supplementary ZIP provides 29 files and 5,633 lines of Python implementing targets, reward combiners, parameter variation, noise, termination logic, reference trajectories, and a notional environment. Its README explicitly says FGE, trained/exported policies, and agent-training infrastructure are absent; simulator/state interfaces return sketches or fake data. All 53 bundled tests pass after installing the four declared dependencies. Seven source-data text files expose plotted line data and JSON, not the underlying raw diagnostic acquisition, while FGE and LIUQE require a license agreement.

anchors.section: Extended Data Table 3 / released reward definitions

key_findings.claim: The evidence supports a landmark expansion of RL magnetic-control scope, but not the broader prospective claims about other tokamaks, reactor optimization, fusion performance, or commercial energy.
key_findings.evidence: All plant evidence comes from the small, flexible TCV research tokamak and short control windows. No controller is transferred to a second device in this paper, and no fusion gain, confinement improvement, heat-load reduction, long-pulse reliability, disruption-rate reduction, reactor-scale operation, or ITER experiment is reported. Joint optimization of shape, wall, heat load, sensors, and reactor performance is presented as future potential.

method.core_idea: Specify desired plasma-current and geometric trajectories as targets and rewards, train a compact target-conditioned coil-voltage policy against many randomized instances of a device-specific free-boundary simulator, and deploy the deterministic policy directly in the TCV real-time control loop without plant-side tuning.
method.mechanism: At 10 kHz the actor maps 92 magnetic/current measurements and up to 132 target values to commands for 19 coils. During training, 5,000 parallel FGE actors simulate circuit-coupled Grad-Shafranov equilibria with randomized plasma, sensor, and actuator parameters. MPO learns from replay using a privileged recurrent critic; the smaller feedforward actor is compiled with unnecessary stochastic computations removed and handed control after conventional plasma formation. Offline LIUQE reconstruction then scores current, boundary, and X-point tracking.
assumptions: Axisymmetric free-boundary equilibrium and lumped current evolution capture the plant dynamics relevant to the demonstrated magnetic-control intervals.
Ranges identified from prior TCV data cover the important plant-model mismatch in plasma parameters, sensors, delays, power supplies, and coil biases.
The 92 deployed signals contain enough information for a feedforward policy to infer the hidden equilibrium state and parameter variation.
Reward components and time-varying targets faithfully encode the operator's true control objective and hardware constraints.
A deterministic mean policy that performs well in simulation retains adequate robustness after stochastic exploration is removed.
Post-shot LIUQE reconstruction is sufficiently accurate and unbiased for evaluating shape and X-point tracking at approximately centimetre scale.
Conventional startup control, device interlocks, and disruption protection remain available outside the learned policy.
The selected successful shots and limited repeatability evidence characterize controller reliability well enough for a feasibility demonstration.
Other tokamaks can supply an adequate simulator, system identification, centralized low-latency computation, startup controller, and safety envelope before transfer is attempted.

techniques.role: Conditions one policy architecture on time-varying plasma-current, boundary, shape-parameter, position, and X-point targets.
Learns a stochastic Gaussian actor and Q-function from replay while supporting high-dimensional continuous coil commands.
Uses a recurrent, privileged, high-capacity critic during training while constraining the deployed feedforward actor to the plant latency budget.
Models coil, vessel, plasma equilibrium, synthetic sensor, and lumped current dynamics for safe high-throughput training.
Varies identified plasma, sensor, actuator, delay, bias, and noise parameters episode by episode to bridge simulation and TCV.
Transforms physical tracking errors and operational preferences into bounded qualities combined by weighted geometric means or smooth aggregators.
Penalizes coil-current regions associated with a nonlinear stuck-power-supply behavior so the policy learns to cross them quickly.
Removes exploration-only outputs and compiles the actor and target table into cache-efficient binary code that runs within 50 microseconds.
Uses LIUQE after each experiment to reconstruct boundary, position, X-points, and derived shape metrics for evaluation.

evaluations.setting: Fundamental sequence on TCV shot 70915, including takeover, current ramp, elongation, vertical motion, triangularity change, and transition to a diverted shape
evaluations.metric: Plasma-current and LCFS-shape RMSE over 0.1-1.0 s
evaluations.result: 0.62 kA current RMSE and 0.75 cm shape RMSE; the diverted phase reaches 0.28 kA and 0.53 cm
evaluations.baseline: Prespecified engineering aims of less than 5 kA current error and less than 2 cm shape error; no matched conventional-controller shot

evaluations.setting: Highly elongated plasma on TCV shot 70920
evaluations.metric: Current, boundary shape, triangularity, elongation, and radius RMSE
evaluations.result: 1.2 kA, 1.6 cm, 0.012, 0.018, and 0.65 cm respectively while reaching elongation 1.9
evaluations.baseline: Target trajectories and tolerance goals; no PID, LQR, or model-based controller comparison

evaluations.setting: ITER-like H-mode shape with neutral-beam heating on TCV shot 70600
evaluations.result: 2.6 kA, 1.4 cm, and 2.1 cm respectively, with beta_p rising to 1.12
evaluations.baseline: Two-shot qualitative repeatability before differing heating conditions in shots 70599 and 70600; no repeated-shot confidence interval

evaluations.setting: Strong negative-triangularity configuration on TCV shot 70457
evaluations.metric: Triangularity, current, boundary shape, elongation, radius, and X-point RMSE
evaluations.result: 0.070, 3.5 kA, 1.3 cm, 0.072, 0.38 cm, and 2.9 cm respectively for a -0.8 target
evaluations.baseline: Target tracking only; no conventional-controller or milder-shape baseline

evaluations.setting: Time-varying snowflake configuration on TCV shot 70755
evaluations.metric: X-point separation trajectory, combined X-point RMSE, current RMSE, and boundary-shape RMSE
evaluations.result: Separation reduced from 34 cm to 6.6 cm; combined X-point error 3.7 cm, current error 0.50 kA, and shape error 0.65 cm
evaluations.baseline: Desired trajectory; the paper cites prior conventional snowflake control but does not run a matched comparison

evaluations.setting: Two independently targeted plasma droplets on TCV shot 69545
evaluations.metric: Sustained control window and qualitative current/image evidence
evaluations.result: Both droplets persist for the full 200 ms learned-control window
evaluations.baseline: No quantitative droplet RMSE, repeatability panel, or conventional-control baseline

evaluations.setting: Simulation ablations for critic recurrence and distributed actor count
evaluations.result: A 256-wide recurrent critic reaches about 95 reward while feedforward critics of 256, 512, and 1,024 units degrade well below it; 100 actors approach 5,000-actor learning speed on basic stabilization, while 20 actors take roughly two days
evaluations.baseline: Symmetric feedforward critics and 100- or 20-actor training configurations

limitations: Author-stated: radial pressure and current-density transport from heating and current drive are not modeled; profile evolution is reduced to polynomial parameters and a lumped current equation.
Author-stated: an existing magnetic controller is required for plasma breakdown and early ramp-up before learned-policy handover.
Author-stated: simulation termination criteria do not guarantee disruption avoidance; devices with low disruption tolerance require an independent fallback controller or protection interlock.
Author-stated: feedforward actors retain steady-state errors; recurrent actors may help but may also overfit the simulator and transfer less reliably.
Reviewer-identified: headline hardware results are one named shot per configuration, with only a two-shot repeatability visualization for one policy and no distribution over success rate or error.
Reviewer-identified: no matched conventional, model-predictive, PID, LQR, or expert-controller baseline is executed under the same shot conditions.
Reviewer-identified: LIUQE's typical approximately 1 cm boundary accuracy is close to several 0.53-1.6 cm reported shape errors, yet reconstruction uncertainty is not propagated.

Reviewer-identified: each experiment changes reward terms, weights, references, and sometimes simulator details, so versatility does not mean one frozen policy or one unchanged objective solved every task.

Reviewer-identified: all hardware demonstrations are on TCV and last at most about one second after handover; transfer across devices, long-pulse stability, reactor conditions, and scaling are untested.
Reviewer-identified: the droplets use a pressureless approximation, an earlier current model, and a disabled G coil, reducing comparability with the single-plasma environment.
Reviewer-identified: compute, simulator-call count, training variance, failed training runs, hyperparameter-search budget, and human reward-design effort are not fully reported.
Reviewer-identified: the artifact omits FGE, trained weights, full MPO infrastructure, the real-time compiler/integration stack, and raw plant acquisition, preventing end-to-end reproduction.
Reviewer-identified: a provisional patent application creates a disclosed commercial-interest context for broad platform claims.
failure_modes: Unmodeled transport or kinetic evolution shifts the heated plasma outside the domain-randomized equilibrium dynamics and causes systematic control error.
The feedforward actor cannot infer a slowly varying hidden state, producing persistent current or shape bias.
A recurrent actor fits simulator-specific temporal signatures and fails more severely than a simpler feedforward policy on the plant.
Power supplies stick near a current-polarity transition not covered by the learned avoidance region.
A target/reward combination is geometrically satisfiable in simulation but drives unsafe q95, coil-current, ohmic-current-difference, or disruption conditions on hardware.
The policy exploits simulator inaccuracies because MPO optimizes reward rather than physical fidelity.
A new tokamak's sensors, coils, delays, vessel currents, or operational-profile range violate the assumptions encoded by the TCV simulator and domain randomization.
LIUQE reconstruction error makes a controller look more or less accurate than it was near the centimetre-scale boundary-error floor.
A compiled target table or plant interface mismatch sends correct network outputs to incorrect coil channels or at incorrect timing.
The learned controller reaches an out-of-distribution plasma state for which no formal safety certificate or recovery policy exists.
Reward aggregation sacrifices a low-weight safety- or physics-relevant objective to improve dominant tracking components while preserving high total reward.
A controller that succeeds in one handpicked discharge proves brittle across shot-to-shot wall, heating, density, or diagnostic variation.
reusable_insights: Separate training-time capacity from deployment-time latency: a recurrent privileged critic can resolve hidden dynamics without burdening the real-time policy.
Treat system identification and domain-randomization ranges as first-class experimental artifacts; sim-to-real success depends as much on these ranges as on the RL algorithm.
Compile target-conditioned policies only after benchmarking exact worst-case latency on the plant processor, including signal-processing and logging budgets.
Use explicit operational termination conditions during training, but never treat reward penalties as a substitute for hard interlocks or a recovery controller.
Measure learned control with an estimator-independent uncertainty budget whenever the reported error approaches the reconstruction system's accuracy floor.
Report controller reliability over repeated hardware shots and matched traditional baselines, not only a gallery of distinct successful capabilities.
Keep reward definitions and control references machine-readable; the released reward and reference code is among the most reusable parts of this work.
Distinguish a model-free optimizer interface from a model-dependent engineering pipeline when training occurs entirely inside a physics simulator.
Ablate task engineering as well as network architecture: reward terms, hardware avoidance rules, and simulator variants can carry substantial problem-specific knowledge.
For future devices, couple learned nominal control to online uncertainty or support detection so the protection layer can identify simulator-domain exits.
open_questions: What is the shot-to-shot success rate and error distribution for each policy across wall conditions, heating levels, densities, and diagnostic perturbations?
How does the learned controller compare with the best TCV conventional or model-based controller under identical references, actuator limits, and reconstruction metrics?
Can one runtime-conditioned policy generalize across the paper's configurations without retraining separate policies and reward setups?
Does a recurrent actor remove steady-state bias while preserving zero-shot plant transfer, and how can simulator overfitting be detected before a shot?
Which domain-randomization components are necessary for transfer, and what plant data justify each range?
How does performance change when radial transport, heating, density evolution, and disruption-relevant physics are added to the training simulator?
Can formal reachability, probabilistic safety certification, or a shielded backup controller provide guarantees around the learned policy?
How much operator time and compute are required to specify rewards, tune ranges, train candidates, validate compiled policies, and obtain one successful new configuration?
Can the end-to-end system be reproduced with an open simulator, released checkpoints, raw shot data, and plant-independent deployment tooling?
Do learned magnetic-control gains translate into improved confinement, heat exhaust, disruption avoidance, pulse duration, or fusion performance rather than tracking alone?
How well does the method scale to ITER-like latency, actuator, diagnostic, and safety constraints, and what evidence would justify first deployment?

competitive_landscape.title: Towards practical reinforcement learning for tokamak magnetic control
competitive_landscape.difference: Tracey et al. build directly on the reviewed TCV architecture, acknowledge its accuracy, steady-state-bias, and training-time disadvantages, and report up to 65% simulated shape-accuracy improvement, reduced current bias, at least threefold faster task learning, and new TCV experiments. It is the closest follow-up and supersedes several practical-performance details of the 2022 system.

competitive_landscape.title: Avoiding fusion plasma tearing instability with deep reinforcement learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Seo et al. train against a learned multimodal dynamics model and deploy on DIII-D to keep tearing-instability likelihood below a threshold while retaining H-mode performance. It addresses disruption-relevant trajectory control beyond boundary shaping, but does not replace the same complete magnetic-control interface.

competitive_landscape.title: High-Fidelity Data-Driven Dynamics Model for Reinforcement Learning-based Magnetic Control in HL-3 Tokamak
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. replace the first-principles training environment with a learned HL-3 dynamics model, train a 17-coil PPO controller in about 22 minutes on an RTX 4090, and report 1 kHz on-device trajectory tracking plus triangularity adaptation. Their own ablation shows poor zero-shot extrapolation to unseen 700 kA operation without a few such shots, exposing a different data-versus-physics generalization tradeoff.

competitive_landscape.title: Demonstration of reconstruction-free static magnetic control of DIII-D plasma with deep reinforcement learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Subbotin et al. deploy a Soft Actor-Critic magnetic controller on the mid-size DIII-D tokamak using NSFsim with equilibrium, circuit, and 1D transport dynamics. It is the strongest later evidence that reconstruction-free learned magnetic control can move beyond TCV, although its published title and scope are static magnetic control rather than the reviewed paper's broad time-varying configuration gallery.

competitive_landscape.title: Offline Reinforcement Learning for Rotation Profile Control in Tokamaks
competitive_landscape.difference: Sonker et al. train offline and offline-model-based policies solely from historical DIII-D data, then deploy a rotation-profile controller on hardware. This tackles an internal-profile problem for which accurate first-principles control simulators are lacking, complementing rather than replacing equilibrium magnetic control while relaxing the reviewed paper's dependence on FGE.

competitive_landscape.title: Reinforcement learning for vertical position control on the EXL-50U spherical tokamak
competitive_landscape.difference: This EXL-50U study reports learned vertical-position takeover in more than ten discharges and compares RL-centered control with operational PID and model-based LQR/LQRI metrics. Its control scope is much narrower, but its multi-shot and matched-baseline design addresses two of the reviewed paper's largest evaluation gaps; PID is best on one transfer ITAE comparison, while integral-augmented RL improves the broader suite.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present a previously undescribed general architecture that learns direct commands for the full set of tokamak coils, transfers zero shot to real hardware, reduces controller-design effort, and handles conventional, advanced, and two-plasma configurations through high-level target specification.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Prior work already applied RL to tokamak profile and feedforward beta control, and conventional TCV controllers already handled advanced snowflake configurations. What the 2022 evidence newly combines is a single compact raw-sensor-to-all-coils feedback interface, simulator-trained asymmetric actor-critic learning, real-time 10 kHz compilation, and hardware demonstrations across a much broader objective family including two simultaneous droplets. Later primary work improves its accuracy and training efficiency and extends learned magnetic or profile control to DIII-D, HL-3, and EXL-50U.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The paper is a landmark systems and experimental integration result for learned tokamak magnetic control, not the first use of RL in a tokamak and not evidence that conventional control, equilibrium modeling, system identification, reward engineering, or safety infrastructure has become unnecessary. Its most defensible novelty is breadth plus zero-shot real-time full-coil hardware control on TCV. Claims of general transfer, minimal design effort, reactor optimization, fusion-performance benefit, and commercial relevance remain prospective.

reviewer_notes: Primary review used the exact 20-page Europe PMC version-of-record mirror matching DOI 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9; all pages, equations, five main figures, five Extended Data figures, five Extended Data tables, Methods, data/code statements, and disclosures were inspected visually and against extracted text. The Nature supplementary bundle was separately audited: one one-page cover PDF, a 29-file Python ZIP, and seven plot-data exports for the main and Extended Data figures. The code contains 5,633 Python lines under Apache-style headers; in a clean temporary virtual environment its 53 bundled tests passed, but several simulator/state paths are explicitly sketches or fake data. The release omits FGE, LIUQE source, learned checkpoints, full training infrastructure, plant compiler/integration, and raw acquisition, so it supports inspection of objectives and scaffolding rather than full reproduction. Competitive primary records were checked through 2026-08-24. Exact table values were transcribed conservatively; centimetre-scale tracking differences are interpreted in light of the paper's stated approximately 1 cm LIUQE boundary accuracy.
